criteria.description: Identifies the discontinuity/wraparound problem (e.g. an angle near 0 and near 2*pi represent nearby rotations but are numerically far apart).
Identifies gimbal lock (or an equivalent description of a 3-parameter representation losing a degree of freedom at certain configurations) as the deeper problem specific to 3D.

commonErrors: Only mentioning that quaternions are 'more compact' or 'easier to compute with' without addressing the actual topological problem being asked about.
Confusing gimbal lock with numerical error accumulation (a different, unrelated issue).

solutions.fullSolution: A direct 3-parameter representation of SO(3) (e.g. Euler angles, or a raw rotation vector without the exponential map structure) has two related problems. First, like an angle in [0, 2*pi) for SO(2), it can have discontinuities: two numerically distant parameter values can represent nearly identical rotations. Second, and more seriously in 3D: at certain orientations (e.g. when the pitch angle in Euler angles reaches +-90 degrees), two of the three rotation axes become aligned, and the representation locally loses a degree of freedom, i.e. gimbal lock. This happens because SO(3) is not topologically equivalent to a flat 3D parameter space (it's a genuinely curved 3-manifold), so no 3-parameter chart can cover it without singularities. S^3 (via the quaternion double-cover) is a smooth, singularity-free 3-manifold, so quaternions avoid gimbal lock entirely, at the cost of one redundant parameter and the constraint |q|=1.

criteria.description: Correctly differentiates q(t) component-wise: qdot(t) = (-1/2 sin(t/2), 1/2 cos(t/2) what).
Correctly applies the concatenation rule to q(t) o (1/2)(0,what), including recognizing that the cross-product term what x what vanishes.
Uses what^T what = 1 (unit axis) to simplify the scalar term and shows the two expressions match exactly.

commonErrors: Forgetting that what is a unit vector, so what^T what = 1, not leaving it as a general dot product.
Sign errors when differentiating sin(t/2) and cos(t/2) (chain rule factor of 1/2 from the argument t/2 is easy to drop).

solutions.fullSolution:
Differentiating q(t) = (cos(t/2), sin(t/2) what) component-wise: qdot(t) = (-1/2 sin(t/2), 1/2 cos(t/2) what).

Now compute q(t) o (1/2)(0, what) using q o q' = (q0 q0' - qbar . q'bar, q0 q'bar + q0' qbar + qbar x q'bar) with q0'=0, q'bar = (1/2) what:
scalar part: cos(t/2)*0 - sin(t/2)what . (1/2)what = -1/2 sin(t/2) (what.what) = -1/2 sin(t/2), since what.what=1.
vector part: cos(t/2)*(1/2)what + 0*sin(t/2)what + sin(t/2)what x (1/2)what = 1/2 cos(t/2) what + 0, since what x what = 0.

So q(t) o (1/2)(0,what) = (-1/2 sin(t/2), 1/2 cos(t/2) what), identical to qdot(t) computed directly. QED.

symbolic.equivalenceNotes: Equivalent forms like (1-q0**2)**0.5 are accepted; the checker verifies numeric equivalence at sampled points, not string matching.

solutions.fullSolution: sin(theta/2) = sin(arccos(q0)) = sqrt(1 - q0^2), by the standard half-angle/Pythagorean identity for arccos. This also matches the geometric fact that |qbar| = sqrt(1-q0^2) for a unit quaternion (since q0^2 + |qbar|^2 = 1), consistent with the reference definition what = qbar/sin(theta/2).

criteria.description: Correctly left-multiplies both sides by q^-1 and uses associativity plus q^-1 o q = I to isolate (1/2)(0,w) on the left.
Correctly solves for w = 2[q^-1 o qdot]_{1:3}.
Correctly explains that setting qdot=e_i for each i=0..3 and evaluating gives the i-th column of J(q), since the relation is linear in qdot.

commonErrors: Trying to divide by q instead of multiplying by q^-1 (quaternion concatenation isn't commutative division in the usual sense, always left- or right-multiply by the inverse explicitly).
Forgetting that only components 1:3 (the vector part) of q^-1 o qdot are taken, since the scalar part of the tangent vector (1/2)(0,w) is always zero.

solutions.fullSolution:
Starting from qdot = q o (1/2)(0,w), left-multiply both sides by q^-1: q^-1 o qdot = q^-1 o q o (1/2)(0,w) = I o (1/2)(0,w) = (1/2)(0,w), using associativity of quaternion concatenation and q^-1 o q = I.

The right-hand side (1/2)(0,w) has vector part (components 1:3) equal to (1/2)w. So taking the vector part of both sides and multiplying by 2: w = 2[q^-1 o qdot]_{1:3}.

This expression is linear in qdot (quaternion concatenation is bilinear). So if we plug in qdot = e_i (the i-th standard basis vector of R^4, i=0,1,2,3), we get w_i := 2[q^-1 o e_i]_{1:3}, which by definition is exactly the i-th column of the matrix J(q) satisfying w = J(q) qdot for ANY qdot, not just the basis vectors, since a linear map is fully determined by its action on a basis.
